title: The Faintest Line
subtitle: A shift on the dye district railway
story:
The dye district made colour for two hundred years, and when the trade died the railway under it went dark. The works has it now: the lichen grows on the tunnel fabric itself, orange and grey-green across the old tile, and it is scraped and racked and sold for pigment. You are on shift, and there are two jobs on the slate.

First, the yield. It has fallen nine seasons running. The works re-seeds from the heaviest growth on the wall every season and the colour keeps thinning, so somebody wants to know which gene actually governs pigment — not which one shouts loudest. The assay is filed from a car's engineer's compartment, and a filed answer is the reason the traffic office energises a line.

Second, find us more wall. The standing order is bigger than the growing face. The network is older than the works and not all of it is on the books. Ride it, keep your eyes open, and note anything you see out there that should not be there.

The river takes the low tunnels on the evening tide. You have one ebb.

puzzleQueue.note: RUNG 1 · pairwise correlation. Which gene is most tightly co-expressed with XAN_4418? ANSWER XAN_4574 (|r| 0.833 vs 0.080 next, 944%). The probe is deliberately a SATELLITE pair — probing inside the pigment module returns XAN_1192 and spoils the boss.

puzzleQueue.label: The assay bench — the control strand
puzzleQueue.note: RUNG 2 · threshold |r|>0.75 + one-vs-all. Which gene has no co-expression partners at all? ANSWER XAN_6246, the sole isolate. State the cutoff explicitly — network structure is threshold-dependent. Every answer is stable across 0.72-0.78.

puzzleQueue.label: The assay bench — the works' standing practice
puzzleQueue.note: RUNG 3 · module + abundance. THE TAUGHT TRAP. Which gene is most abundant in the pigment module? ANSWER XAN_1815 (1434 vs 245, 486%) — which has DEGREE 1. This is the method the works has re-seeded by for nine seasons while the colour thinned out.

puzzleQueue.label: The assay bench — the regulator
puzzleQueue.note: RUNG 4 · BOSS. module + network position. Which gene regulates pigment production? ANSWER XAN_1192 — the LOWEST-EXPRESSED gene in the dataset, rank 24 of 24, connected to every other gene in its module (degree 7 vs 4). Decoy: XAN_3514, loudest in the transcriptome at 5644 units, degree 3, a bystander.

debrief.title: How this railway worked
debrief.intro: Two networks, and they had nothing to do with each other. The genes' network you built yourself — correlate, threshold, read. The rails' network was handed to you as observed fact, one ride at a time, and you could only ever know the parts of it you had been down. Both times the loudest thing was not the most connected thing.

worldPlatePrompt: A wide establishing view inside a Victorian underground railway that stood derelict for a century and is now being worked again as a lichen farm. TIME-NEUTRAL soft even underground light, neither dawn nor dusk, no daylight in this frame. THE CROP IS THE ARCHITECTURE, AND THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING IN THE FRAME: the lichen grows ON THE FABRIC OF THE TUNNEL ITSELF, not in containers — thick living sheets of flat orange rosettes and swollen grey-green crusts spreading across the glazed wall tile, climbing the pilasters and furring the brick soffits of the arches overhead, so the walls themselves are visibly alive and shaggy with it. It is a crop growing on a building. Galvanised racking and plastic trays of cut crust stand about as the HARVEST TAKEN OFF THOSE WALLS — the product, never the source. Nothing is cultivated in a tray. THE FABRIC UNDER IT IS OLD AND DAMAGED: glazed brick and tile in ochre, saffron and dirty cream, much of it crazed, chipped or missing with the bedding mortar showing through; paint peeling in sheets off cast-iron columns; rust and water stains bleeding down; perished cable looped on old porcelain insulators; sooted segmental brick arches; granite platform edges worn hollow. A CREW WORKS HERE NOW, VISIBLY AND WELL: cheap bright LED work-lamps on yellow flex strung along the arches, duckboards laid over the wet, cable ties and gaffer tape, a kettle and enamel mugs on a plank shelf, a coat on a hook, and notices, work rotas, tally sheets and curling postcards tacked and taped to the tile with chalked marks and scratched tallies beside them. Repairs done with ingenuity — a propped timber, a patched panel, a hose run into a channel. TWO COLOUR TEMPERATURES, AND BOTH MUST BE STRONGLY PRESENT — this must NOT be a monochrome amber or sepia picture. WARM: pools of amber lamplight around the work-lamps and the crew's corner. COLD: everywhere the lamps do not reach, a distinct COLD BLUE-GREEN DAMP — wet black tile going blue in the shadow, green-black standing water, cold blue-green light down the tunnel mouths and in the depths of the arches, the chill of a place with a river behind the wall. The cold blue-green should occupy at least as much of the frame as the warm amber, and the two should meet in clear contrast rather than blending into brown. Damp air, faint haze, film grain. Photographic and beautiful. THE MOOD IS WARM, PURPOSEFUL AND CHARACTERFUL — a magnificent run-down place that a good crew has taken on and made theirs. It is emphatically NOT eerie, NOT spooky, NOT creepy, NOT haunted, NOT menacing, NOT post-apocalyptic and NOT an abandoned ruin. Dark and dirty in places, and still plainly and warmly worked in. No cobwebs, no gloom for its own sake, no horror atmosphere of any kind. No large blank empty wall areas — every surface carries the marks and clutter of a working place. No people, no lettering, no captions, no text, no signage or readable writing of any kind anywhere. No sepia monochrome, no uniform brown or orange cast over the whole image.
